book.title: Big Magic: Creative Living Beyond Fear
book.author: Elizabeth Gilbert

confidence_note: Gilbert's theory that ideas are disembodied energies seeking human collaborators is central to Big Magic, and she illustrates it with a well-known story: she began a novel about a woman from Minnesota drawn into a doomed highway project in the Amazon jungle in the 1960s, set it aside for a long time because of life events, and when she returned the idea was gone. Later she learned her friend Ann Patchett was writing a novel set in the Amazon with strikingly similar elements (which became State of Wonder). The two had met at a public event and shared a kiss on the cheek, which Gilbert playfully suggests is when the idea passed from her to Patchett. Details are paraphrased.
facts: Gilbert proposes that ideas are a kind of disembodied life form, seeking a human collaborator to bring them into the world.
If you are not available, an idea may eventually move on and look for someone else.
She once began a novel about a middle-aged woman from Minnesota, in love with her married boss, who gets drawn into a doomed highway project in the Amazon jungle in the 1960s.
Life circumstances pulled her away from the book for a long time. When she returned, the idea had gone cold; she couldn't bring it back to life.
Around then she became friends with the novelist Ann Patchett. They had first met at a public event, where they shared a kiss on the cheek.
Later Gilbert learned that Patchett was writing a novel set in the Amazon, about a Minnesotan woman in love with her married boss, with strikingly similar elements. It became State of Wonder.
Gilbert jokes that the idea passed to Patchett with that kiss. Her point: when an idea comes to you, treat it seriously and give it your attention while it's there.
tension: An idea you neglect may not wait for you forever.
opening_idea: Two novelists meet and exchange a kiss on the cheek. Later, one of them writes the other's abandoned novel.

lessons.idea: Ideas come with a kind of invitation that expires.
lessons.anchor: The Amazon novel that went cold

lessons.idea: An idea is best honored by working on it.

lessons.idea: Holding ideas lightly makes you generous rather than jealous.
lessons.anchor: Gilbert's playful response to Patchett's novel

reflect: Which idea have you been carrying without acting on?
What would it take to give it one hour this week?
reflect_final: If an idea of yours were looking for someone else to bring it to life, which one would leave first?

use_cases.situation: You have a side-project idea you keep postponing.
use_cases.move: Give it a regular weekly slot now, before it goes cold.

use_cases.situation: A teammate's idea keeps getting parked in meetings.
use_cases.move: Assign an owner and a first small step before the meeting ends.

use_cases.situation: A friend is upset that someone else launched 'their' idea.
use_cases.move: Share Gilbert's story and ask which idea they'll commit to now.
